The Island imperial pigeon (Ducula pistrinaria) is a large, frugivorous columbid endemic to the lowland forests of Melanesia, and its life-history traits reflect a characteristically slow pace of life for a bird of this size. Field measurements of incubating adults, recorded at an ambient temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], indicate a resting metabolic rate of 193 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 193 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that is relatively modest given the species' body mass and suggests an energy-conserving physiology adapted to a diet of energy-dilute fruits. Newly hatched chicks emerge from the egg at a surprisingly low initial wet weight of just 29.7 grams [Ww0 = 29.7 grams], representing a small fraction of the adult mass and underscoring the altricial nature of the neonate. This minimal starting mass necessitates a prolonged period of intensive parental provisioning, during which the nestling undergoes a dramatic increase in size.

As the nestling develops under the same warm thermal conditions typical of tropical lowland environments, its growth trajectory is remarkably rapid, culminating in a fledging event that occurs precisely 27 days after hatching [tx = 27 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This developmental milestone, attained at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], marks the point at which the chick achieves its first sustained flight and leaves the nest, although it remains dependent on its parents for food for some time thereafter. The age at hatching itself, or the incubation period, has been recorded at exactly 27 days [ab = 27 days] based on comparative data from the closely related Torresian imperial pigeon (Ducula spilorrhoa), and this duration is consistent across the two species when eggs are maintained at a steady temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This relatively long incubation period is typical of the genus.

Following the fledgling stage, the juvenile bird enters a protracted period of growth and physiological maturation before it can reproduce. Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal development and the ability to produce viable gametes, is reached at 78 days after hatching [tp = 78 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime of 40.5 °C, a temperature that sustains the physiological processes of growth in these tropical birds at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This suggests that the development of the reproductive system is largely completed within the first three months of life. However, the attainment of sexual maturity does not immediately translate into successful breeding, as young birds must first acquire a territory, secure a mate, and develop the foraging skills necessary to support the energetic demands of egg production and chick-rearing. Consequently, a significant lag exists between pubertal development and actual reproductive output, a phenomenon widely documented among columbids of similar body mass that inhabit resource-limited island environments.

The first successful brood is not typically initiated until the bird is much older, with the age at first reproduction estimated at 949 days since birth [tR = 949 days since birth], a figure derived from field observations of banded populations at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This delay, occurring at an ambient temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], is a common life-history feature among large columbids and is interpreted as a period of deferred maturity during which individuals refine their foraging efficiency and establish a stable breeding position. Once a female begins breeding, her reproductive output is constrained by the species' low fecundity schedule. Females lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and they typically produce just one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year], a rate that is among the lowest recorded for any pigeon species of comparable body mass. This exceptionally low reproductive output, under the same thermal conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], places Ducula pistrinaria at the extreme slow end of the life-history continuum within the Columbidae.

The maximum lifespan recorded for this species in the wild is approximately 5,877 days [am = approximately 5,877 days], which translates to just over sixteen years when maintained at a typical environmental temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This extended longevity is a hallmark of a slow life-history strategy, where high adult survival compensates for an exceptionally low annual reproductive rate. The ultimate wet weight for adult females reaches an average of 513 grams [Wwi = 513 grams], a size that places Ducula pistrinaria among the larger members of its genus and necessitates a high absolute food intake. This substantial adult body mass, combined with a single-egg clutch and a single annual breeding attempt, results in a very low intrinsic rate of population increase, making the species particularly vulnerable to habitat loss and overhunting throughout its island range.
